title: The Afternoon Brief: FIFA's private equity plan now mathematically blocked
dek: Three confederations representing 143 of FIFA's 211 votes have rejected Infantino's plan to bring private investors into the World Cup, as two senior officials broke publicly with the proposal and Chelsea absorbed a £10m fine for agent payment violations.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The FIFA private equity plan cannot pass under current voting rules with three confederations opposed, but the reporting does not say how Infantino intends to respond before the Sept. 19 deadline.
bottom_line: Three FIFA confederations representing 143 of 211 member votes now stand opposed to Infantino's private equity plan, and two senior FIFA officials, adviser Carlos Cordeiro and chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, have broken publicly with the proposal on governance and trust grounds. Elsewhere the day carried a £10m FA fine against Chelsea for agent payment violations spanning 2009-2022, four NFL training camp holdouts including Bijan Robinson and Jahmyr Gibbs, a WNBA trade sending Aneesah Morrow to Toronto ahead of Sunday's deadline, and tributes following the death of AC Milan great Franco Baresi at 66. The reporting establishes the scale of FIFA opposition clearly but does not say how Infantino intends to respond before the Sept. 19 deadline. The Aug. 14 World Cup expansion decision, Sunday's WNBA trade deadline, and the Nov. 18 challenger deadline are the nearest checkpoints on the calendar.
body: The day's central fact has not changed since morning but has hardened: UEFA, Concacaf, and the AFC together represent 143 of FIFA's 211 member associations, and all three have now rejected Gianni Infantino's plan to bring private investors into a $20 billion commercial subsidiary covering World Cup and Club World Cup rights. That bloc is large enough to block the proposal without further defections. What is new since the morning brief is the shape of the internal fallout: Carlos Cordeiro, a senior FIFA adviser and former U.S. Soccer president who sat on the White House World Cup Task Force, resigned Friday in protest, and Kevin Lamour, FIFA's chief operating officer since 2024, publicly accused Infantino of deceiving staff over the proposal and said he would accept losing his job rather than see it advance.

Alongside the FIFA story, the day carried a mix of discipline, business, and roster news. The Football Association fined Chelsea £10m and imposed a suspended two-window registration ban for breaching agent payment rules across a 13-year span from 2009 to 2022, though the conditions that would trigger the suspended ban were not specified. FIFA separately opened a 15-day consultation on expanding the men's World Cup to 64 teams starting in 2030, with a decision targeted for Aug. 14, a date that lands roughly five weeks before Infantino's Sept. 19 deadline for member associations to weigh in on the private equity plan. In the NFL, four players, Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs, Vita Vea, and Tuli Tuipulotu, are holding in from training camp over contract terms; Gibbs and Robinson are each in their second day, and Lions coach Dan Campbell said Gibbs has a minor back issue after a conditioning test Wednesday but is not concerned about the standoff. The WNBA's midseason trade activity began with Toronto acquiring forward Aneesah Morrow from Connecticut in exchange for the rights to Maria Kliundikova and a 2028 second-round pick, ahead of Sunday's deadline. Oregon State women's basketball players filed a union petition with Oregon's state labor board, testing a legal pathway based on public sector law rather than federal jurisdiction. In hockey, Färjestad BK of the Swedish Elite League rescinded defenseman Cal Foote's contract after stakeholder objections tied to his acquittal in a 2018 Hockey Canada case. And AC Milan confirmed the death of Franco Baresi, the club's captain for 15 seasons across a 20-year career that included six Serie A titles and three European Cup triumphs.

The driver behind the FIFA story, as far as the reporting establishes, is a combination of governance concern and financial skepticism: Cordeiro called the deal one that mortgages football's future without compelling justification, and Lamour framed it as the project of one person rather than a considered institutional plan. The reporting does not say whether Infantino has responded to either official directly, nor what internal process FIFA would use to formally approve or reject the restructuring.
No league or FIFA scoreboards were available this cycle, so the numbers above come directly from the day's reporting rather than a live data feed.

The nearer checkpoints are Sunday's WNBA trade deadline, the Aug. 6 Hall of Game preseason opener that the four NFL holdouts are working against, and the Aug. 14 World Cup expansion decision. Further out, the Sept. 19 deadline for FIFA member associations to weigh in on the private equity plan and the Nov. 18 deadline for presidential challengers stand as the points that would show whether Cordeiro and Lamour's public breaks turn into a broader institutional response.
